newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia power struggle keeps PGM market guessing.
newsitem.headline: Russia power struggle keeps PGM market guessing.

text.p: A power struggle among Russian entities for control over multi-billion-dollar platinum group metal (PGM) exports is intensifying, despite Russia's resumption of supplies to the world's top buyer, sources said on Tuesday.

"It sounds as though there are still some unresolved tensions and power struggles," said Tony Warwick-Ching of CRU International in London. "We should not necessarily assume plain sailing from now on."

Russian precious metals export agency Almazjuvelirexport confirmed on Tuesday it had resumed long-delayed deliveries of platinum group metals to Japan after a nearly seven-month delay, with the first supplies leaving on July 8.
Russia is the world's largest palladium supplier and second largest platinum supplier, with Japan the biggest consumer of both metals.
Sergei Gorny, a deputy director at Almaz, said renewed deliveries showed the agency had resumed normal work after what he said was the disruptive effect of a cabinet reshuffle in March.
"Russia has enough metal to supply world demand for a long time," he said, declining to be more specific. "And our constant partners with whom we work on long-term contracts know this."
But sources said jittery markets might need time to believe the same scenario would not be repeated in the future, adding Almaz might not even be around next year.
"It looks as though there is an interest in keeping the market guessing and keeping upside pressure on prices," added Warwick-Ching.
But Gorny said Almaz had gained room for manoeuvre and was able to act more flexibly this year since the agency was for the first time not required to export exactly what the government had ordered.

"There is a difference this year -- we have an amount that we may sell, not that we are required to sell," he said, adding the agency could only sell less, not more, than ordered by the government. "It's more flexible this year for us."
He said Almaz would do its best to make sure this year's events were not repeated in 1998 and that work on contracts for next year had already begun.

World prices for palladium, used in catalytic convertors, dentistry and electronics, spiked to 17-year highs in June, while platinum, popular in jewellery, also soared on jitters over when Russia would resume supplies.

A four-way struggle has shaped up between Almaz, the Finance Ministry, giant metals group Norilsk Nickel and the central bank for control over white metal exports, the details of which are one of Russia's most lucrative and best-kept secrets.
Norilsk Nickel produces nearly all Russia's platinum group metals and is keen to export its output rather than simply sell it to the state at fixed prices and let Almaz do the job.
A senior metals official said Russia was selling exclusively from central bank reserves, and not from Norilsk Nickel or the state strategic reserve Gokhran.
"There were no central bank sales last year, but there arose the necessity of such sales this year," added Vladimir Rybkin, head of the Finance Ministry's precious metals department.

But Gorny said there was no reason to worry about Russia's supply levels, which markets have long suspected are dwindling as Moscow unloaded reserves in previous years to raise cash to bolster economic reforms.
"Speculators, including possibly funds but not limited to them, are the ones who started the hysteria on reserves (being depleted)," Gorny said. "But it doesn't correspond to reality."
